entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a cosine A cos(omega t + phi) into the phasor A angle phi, preserving amplitude and phase for same-frequency phasor addition.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Writing a Zero-Phase Cosine as a Phasor

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $8\cos(\omega t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A zero-phase cosine keeps the same amplitude and becomes a phasor with angle $0$. The shared angular frequency $\omega$ stays outside the phasor, so the correct answer is $8\angle 0$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $3\cos(\omega t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A cosine with no phase shift maps to $A\angle 0$. Here the amplitude is $3$, so the phasor is $3\angle 0$.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Writing a Positive-Phase Cosine as a Phasor

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $6\cos(\omega t+\pi/4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the rule $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)\mapsto A\angle\phi$. Here the amplitude is $6$ and the positive phase is $\pi/4$, so the phasor is $6\angle\pi/4$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $3\cos(\omega t+2\pi/3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the same phasor rule $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)\mapsto A\angle\phi$. The amplitude is $3$ and the phase is $2\pi/3$, so the phasor is $3\angle 2\pi/3$.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Writing a Negative-Phase Cosine as a Phasor

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $8\cos(\omega t-\pi/4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the rule $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)\mapsto A\angle\phi$. The amplitude stays $8$, and the negative phase stays in the angle, so the phasor is $8\angle-\pi/4$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $7\cos(\omega t-2\pi/3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the same phasor rule: keep the amplitude and move the phase into the angle. Here the amplitude is $7$ and the phase is $-2\pi/3$, so the phasor is $7\angle-2\pi/3$.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Separating the Shared Angular Frequency from the Phasor

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $7\cos(\omega_1 t+\pi/6)$? Keep $\omega_1$ separate from the phasor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude is $7$ and the phase is $\pi/6$, so the cosine becomes the phasor $7\angle\pi/6$. The shared angular frequency $\omega_1$ stays outside the phasor value.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor form of $18\cos(\Omega t-\pi/3)$? Keep $\Omega$ separate from the phasor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude is $18$ and the phase is $-\pi/3$, so the phasor is $18\angle-\pi/3$. The shared angular frequency $\Omega$ is not part of the phasor.

entries.lesson_core_move: Add same-frequency cosines by recognizing their common angular frequency, converting each cosine to its phasor, and summing the phasors as complex quantities.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Recognizing a Common Angular Frequency

prompt_blocks.text: What is the common angular frequency in $8\cos(6t+\pi/4)+3\cos(6t-\pi/7)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the coefficient of $t$ in each cosine argument. Both terms use $6t$, so the shared angular frequency is $6$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the common angular frequency in $5\cos(4t-\pi/8)+11\cos(4t+\pi/3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The coefficient of $t$ is $4$ in both cosine arguments, so the common angular frequency is $4$. The amplitudes and phase shifts do not change that shared frequency.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Converting Each Cosine to a Phasor

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor-sum form of $6\cos(4t+\pi/3)+2\cos(4t-\pi/6)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both cosines share $\omega=4$, so the step is only a notation conversion. Keep the amplitudes and phases together: $6\cos(4t+\pi/3)\mapsto 6\angle\pi/3$ and $2\cos(4t-\pi/6)\mapsto 2\angle-\pi/6$.
The shared angular frequency stays separate; it does not get inserted into the phasor values. So the phasor-sum form is $6\angle\pi/3 + 2\angle-\pi/6$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor-sum form of $3\cos(6t)+5\cos(6t-\pi/2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cosine terms already share $\omega=6$, so convert each term directly to a phasor. The zero-phase term becomes $3\angle0$, and the second term becomes $5\angle-\pi/2$.
Do not move the $6$ into the phasor or change the phase sign. The phasor-sum form is $3\angle0 + 5\angle-\pi/2$.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Forming the Resultant Phasor Sum

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is the resultant phasor sum for $4\cos(3t)+6\cos(3t-\pi/3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The two cosines share the same angular frequency $3$, so convert each one to a phasor and add them directly. The correct resultant phasor sum is $4\angle 0 + 6\angle(-\pi/3)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is the resultant phasor sum for $6\cos(5t)+2\cos(5t-\pi/2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shared angular frequency is $5$, so the two terms become phasors with amplitudes and phases read off directly from the cosines. Keep the result in phasor form: $6\angle 0 + 2\angle(-\pi/2)$.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Adding More Than Two Same-Frequency Cosine Phasors

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor-sum form of $5\cos(4t)+2\cos(4t+\pi/6)+7\cos(4t-\pi/3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: All three terms share the same angular frequency $4$, so each cosine converts to its own phasor without dropping any term.
The correct choice keeps all three amplitudes and all three phases. The wrong choices either drop a term, flip phase signs, collapse the sum into one number, or change the shared frequency.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the phasor-sum form of $3\cos(6t-\pi/4)+4\cos(6t)+2\cos(6t+\pi/2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shared angular frequency is $6$, so the phasor form must preserve all three terms with their original amplitudes and phases.
The other choices either drop a term, flip a phase sign, collapse the amplitudes into one phasor, or change the common frequency from $6$ to $7$.

entries.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the rectangular-form phasor sum for same-frequency cosines by resolving each phasor into real and imaginary components and adding corresponding components.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Adding Axis-Aligned Phasor Components

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $2 + j0$ and $0 + j4$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. The real total is $2 + 0$, and the imaginary total is $0 + 4$.
So the rectangular-form sum is $2 + j4$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $-3 + j0$ and $0 - j5$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: These phasors are already in rectangular form, so preserve the signs and add the real and imaginary parts separately. The real total is $-3 + 0$, and the imaginary total is $0 + (-5)$.
So the rectangular-form sum is $-3 - j5$.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Resolving Two Cosine Phasors into Rectangular Components

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $8\cos(\omega t + 30^\circ)$ and $4\cos(\omega t - 60^\circ)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert each cosine to a phasor, then resolve the phasors into rectangular components and add real parts to real parts and imaginary parts to imaginary parts.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $7\cos(\omega t - 60^\circ)$ and $5\cos(\omega t + 30^\circ)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert both cosines to phasors, resolve each phasor into rectangular form, and then add the real and imaginary parts separately.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Adding Phasors with Negative Rectangular Components

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $(-6 - j1)$ and $(2 + j4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep the signs on each component and add real parts to real parts and imaginary parts to imaginary parts.
So the rectangular-form sum is $-4 + j3$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $(3 - j8)$ and $(-5 + j2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add the real parts together and the imaginary parts together. Do not change the signs before adding.
So the rectangular-form sum is $-2 - j6$.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Adding More Than Two Same-Frequency Phasors in Rectangular Form

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $2 + j0$, $-3 + j4$, and $5 - j1$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add the real parts and imaginary parts separately. The real parts give $2 + (-3) + 5 = 4$, and the imaginary parts give $0 + 4 + (-1) = 3$.
So the rectangular-form sum is $4 + j3$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the rectangular-form sum of $4 + j0$, $-1 + j3$, $2 - j2$, and $-3 + j1$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Collect the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. The real parts give $4 + (-1) + 2 + (-3) = 2$, and the imaginary parts give $0 + 3 + (-2) + 1 = 2$.
So the rectangular-form sum is $2 + j2$.

entries.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a rectangular phasor sum into polar magnitude-angle form so the resultant sinusoid's amplitude and phase can be read from the phasor.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Computing the Magnitude of a Rectangular Phasor Sum

prompt_blocks.text: Given $Z = (5 + j2) + (1 + j3)$, what is $|Z|$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: First combine the rectangular parts: $Z = (5 + j2) + (1 + j3) = 6 + j5$. Then apply the magnitude formula $|Z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ with $a = 6$ and $b = 5$, which gives $|Z| = \sqrt{6^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{61}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $Z = (2 + j5) + (3 + j7)$, what is $|Z|$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combine the components first: $Z = (2 + j5) + (3 + j7) = 5 + j12$. Then compute the magnitude with $|Z| = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13$.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Computing the Reference Angle of a Rectangular Phasor Sum

prompt_blocks.text: For $Z = -3 - 4j$, what is the reference angle of $Z$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use absolute values in the ratio, so the sign pattern does not change the acute angle itself. Here $|b|/|a| = 4/3$, so the reference angle is $\tan^{-1}(4/3)$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $Z = -5 + 12j$, what is the reference angle of $Z$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, use absolute values in the reference-angle ratio. Here $|b|/|a| = 12/5$, so the acute reference angle is $\tan^{-1}(12/5)$; the quadrant-adjusted angle comes later.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Choosing the Correct Quadrant for the Phasor Angle

prompt_blocks.text: If $Z = -2 - 2j$, what is $\arg(Z)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signs put $Z$ in quadrant III. The reference angle is $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}(|-2|/|-2|) = \pi/4$, so the principal angle is $-\pi + \theta_{\text{ref}} = -3\pi/4$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $Z = 1 - \sqrt{3}j$, what is $\arg(Z)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signs put $Z$ in quadrant IV. The reference angle is $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}/1) = \pi/3$, so the principal angle is $-\theta_{\text{ref}} = -\pi/3$.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Writing the Polar Phasor Sum and Reading Its Magnitude and Angle

prompt_blocks.text: What is the polar form of $Z = -1 - \sqrt{3}j$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude is $|Z| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-\sqrt{3})^2} = 2$. Since both parts are negative, the phasor is in quadrant III, so the principal phase is $-\frac{2\pi}{3}$. Therefore the polar form is $2\angle -\frac{2\pi}{3}$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the polar form of $Z = -1 + \sqrt{3}j$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude is $|Z| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2} = 2$. Since $a < 0$ and $b > 0$, the phasor is in quadrant II, so the principal phase is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$. Therefore the polar form is $2\angle \frac{2\pi}{3}$.

entries.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a polar phasor sum back into a single same-frequency sinusoid by mapping magnitude to amplitude and angle to phase at the common angular frequency.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Identifying the Sinusoid Amplitude from Phasor Magnitude

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $9\angle -40^\circ$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Which amplitude should the equivalent cosine use?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude comes from the phasor magnitude. Here the magnitude is $9$, so the equivalent cosine uses amplitude $9$; the angle $-40^\circ$ and the common angular frequency do not change that step.

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $6\angle -\pi/2$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=5$. Which amplitude should the equivalent cosine use?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The phasor magnitude is $6$, so the amplitude is $6$. The angle $-\pi/2$ and the stated common angular frequency $\omega_0=5$ are context, not the amplitude.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Identifying the Sinusoid Phase from Phasor Angle

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $6\angle \pi/6$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Which phase should the equivalent cosine use?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The phase is the phasor angle. Read $\pi/6$ directly from the polar notation, and leave the amplitude $6$ and the common angular frequency $\omega_0$ unchanged.

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $8\angle -\pi/4$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Which phase should the equivalent cosine use?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The phase is the angle in the phasor. Keep the sign negative, read $-\pi/4$ as the phase, and leave the amplitude $8$ and the common angular frequency $\omega_0$ unchanged.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Preserving the Common Angular Frequency in the Sinusoid

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $6\angle \pi/4$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=4$. Which cosine keeps the frequency exactly as given?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude gives the amplitude and the angle gives the phase, but the common angular frequency must stay $4$. So the cosine keeps $4t$ in the argument.

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $2\angle -\pi/3$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Which cosine keeps the frequency exactly as given?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude is $2$ and the phase is $-\pi/3$, but the symbol $\omega_0$ must pass through unchanged. The correct cosine keeps that exact frequency term.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Writing the Complete Cosine from a Polar Phasor Sum

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $6\angle \pi/3$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=5$. Which cosine is exactly equivalent?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude gives the amplitude $6$, the angle gives the phase $\pi/3$, and the common angular frequency stays $5$. So the cosine is $x(t)=6\cos(5t+\pi/3)$.

prompt_blocks.text: A phasor sum is $12\angle -\pi/6$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=3$. Which cosine is exactly equivalent?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude gives the amplitude $12$, the angle gives the phase $-\pi/6$, and the common angular frequency stays $3$. So the cosine is $x(t)=12\cos(3t-\pi/6)$.

entries.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Express a same-frequency sinusoidal sum in amplitude-phase form by adding component phasors and converting the resultant magnitude and angle into the combined amplitude and phase.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Combining Two Same-Frequency Cosines into One Cosine

prompt_blocks.text: Combine $3\cos(8t+\pi/6)$ and $2\cos(8t-\pi/3)$ into one cosine in amplitude-phase form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert each cosine to a phasor at the shared frequency $8$, add the phasors, and read the result back as one cosine. The sum has magnitude $\sqrt{13}$ and a small negative phase, so the combined cosine is $\sqrt{13}\cos\left(8t-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{2+3\sqrt3}\right)\right)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Combine $5\cos(8t+\pi/6)$ and $2\cos(8t-\pi/3)$ into one cosine in amplitude-phase form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert both terms to phasors at the shared frequency $8$, add them, and convert the result back to amplitude-phase form. The phasor sum has magnitude $\sqrt{29}$ and a positive phase, so the combined cosine is $\sqrt{29}\cos\left(8t+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5-2\sqrt3}{5\sqrt3+2}\right)\right)$.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Finding the Resultant Amplitude and Phase from Component Phasors

prompt_blocks.text: The component phasors are $6-j1$ and $-2+j5$. What is the amplitude-phase form of the combined sinusoid?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add the rectangular parts separately: $(6-j1)+(-2+j5)=4+j4$.
So the combined sinusoid has amplitude $4\sqrt2$ and phase $\pi/4$.

prompt_blocks.text: The component phasors are $3+j2$ and $1-j5$. What is the amplitude-phase form of the combined sinusoid?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add the rectangular parts separately: $(3+j2)+(1-j5)=4-j3$.
So the combined sinusoid has amplitude $5$ and phase $-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)$.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Keeping the Correct Quadrant for the Resultant Phase

prompt_blocks.text: Convert the phasor sum $-3+j4$ into the amplitude-phase form of the corresponding cosine.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude is $\sqrt{(-3)^2+4^2}=5$. Since the real part is negative and the imaginary part is positive, the phasor is in quadrant II, so the phase must be $\pi-\tan^{-1}(4/3)$ rather than the principal arctangent alone.

prompt_blocks.text: Convert the phasor sum $-4-j3$ into the amplitude-phase form of the corresponding cosine.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude is $\sqrt{(-4)^2+(-3)^2}=5$. Because both parts are negative, the phasor lies in quadrant III, so the phase is the principal-angle form $-\pi+\tan^{-1}(3/4)$. Using only $\tan^{-1}(3/4)$ would miss the quadrant correction.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Combining More Than Two Same-Frequency Cosines

prompt_blocks.text: Combine $3\cos(5t)+2\cos(5t+\pi/3)+2\cos(5t+2\pi/3)$ into one cosine in amplitude-phase form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: All three terms share the same angular frequency $5$, so convert each cosine to a phasor and add them in rectangular form.

That phasor is in Quadrant I, so its magnitude is $\sqrt{21}$ and its phase is $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\right)$. The combined cosine is $\sqrt{21}\cos\left(5t+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\right)\right)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Combine $2\cos(6t+\pi)+2\cos(6t+\pi/3)+2\cos(6t+2\pi/3)$ into one cosine in amplitude-phase form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shared angular frequency is $6$, so add the phasors and keep the frequency fixed.
That phasor is in Quadrant II, so the phase is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and the magnitude is $4$. The combined cosine is $4\cos\left(6t+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$.
